title: Wedding horse songs
hook: Guru Ram Das pictures the body as a horse the Lord made, ridden home to the Beloved (Vadhans M4, ang 575)

segments.voice: Yesterday we finished Guru Ram Das's salok on the Gursikh: blessing others, and the Guru asking for the dust of the feet of the one who helps others remember. Your line was help others remember. Did your message go out? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-five.

A drum, a crowd in bright clothes, and a groom climbing onto a decorated horse while the women of his family sing. In Punjabi wedding tradition, the songs sung around the groom and his horse have a name: ghorian, horse songs. They're family songs, teasing and proud, the kind aunts know by heart. Guru Ram Das took that wedding song and wrote his own, in Raga Vadhans. Same horse, same joy, same ride to the bride's door. But the rider, and the road, and the one waiting at the end, all change. Today's word is the horse songs.
screen: `A GROOM ON A DECORATED HORSE.` → `GHORIAN: THE HORSE SONGS.` → `THE GURU WRITES HIS OWN.`

segments.voice: Here's how his Ghorian open, paraphrased. The body is a horse, fashioned by the Lord. Blessed is this human life, received by good fortune. And then: this body is the horse on which the Lord is reached. Meeting the True Guru, songs of joy are sung. Four things happen in those few lines. First, the borrowing. He doesn't invent a new form. He takes a song people already sing at weddings and lets it carry the Name. Second, the horse is the body. Not a prison, not an enemy to be beaten into line. A horse the Lord made, and a gift, the hymn says, received by good fortune. A body is how you get anywhere. Third, the ride. At a wedding, the groom rides to the bride. In the hymn, the ride is the soul going home to the Beloved, the Lord. The whole of a human life becomes the wedding procession, and the body is the horse that carries it there. Fourth, the songs of joy. In the hymn, they're sung on meeting the True Guru. The ride isn't a grim march. It has music in it, the way a baraat, the groom's wedding procession, does. What's striking is how gentle this picture is. A rider who hates the horse doesn't get far. A rider who knows the horse is a gift, feeds it, rests it, and points it the right way, gets to the wedding. That's today's word: ghorian, the horse songs, and the body as the Guru sees it in them.
screen: `A WEDDING SONG CARRIES THE NAME.` · `THE BODY: A HORSE THE LORD MADE.` · `THE RIDE HOME TO THE BELOVED.` · `SONGS OF JOY ON THE WAY.` · then, large: `GHORIAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ride your body kindly. In the sit, let the breath slow and check in with the horse. Start at the feet and move up: legs, back, shoulders, jaw. Where is it tired? Where is it carrying more than it needs to? Thank it once, plainly, for getting you this far. Then choose one kind thing to give it today: water, a walk, an early night. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Ghorian. The wedding horse songs. In Guru Ram Das's hymns in Vadhans, the horse is the body the Lord made, and the ride is the soul's way home. Today's word.
Your line: ride to the beloved. Give your horse the one kind thing you chose, and notice how the ride goes after. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Guru Ram Das's Ghorian are sung in kirtan in Raga Vadhans, and Sikh teachers read them as a picture of the human body as a gift for the soul's journey to God.
